analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans sulfide-ore copper mining on 225,504 acres upstream of the Boundary Waters.
analysis.headline: The bill to make a permanent mining ban around the Boundary Waters has sat in the House Natural Resources Committee since January 2025 with no vote scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill turns a 2023 executive-branch decision into law: about 225,504 acres of federal land and water in Minnesota's Rainy River Watershed, just upstream of the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness and Voyageurs National Park, would be withdrawn from copper-nickel sulfide mining and other mineral development. It leaves existing claims untouched and still allows sand, gravel, granite, iron ore, and taconite removal if it would not harm the watershed. The goal is to keep acid mine drainage out of one of the country's most pristine wilderness areas.
analysis.who_benefits: People who use and value the Boundary Waters: canoeists, anglers, outfitters and tourism businesses in northeastern Minnesota, and three Ojibwe bands whose treaty rights cover the area. The bill's findings cite a study projecting 1,500 to 4,600 more tourism-related jobs and $100 million to $900 million more income over 20 years with a mining ban than without one [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Tourism workers, paddlers, and Ojibwe bands

how_it_helps.text: Withdraws about 225,504 acres of federal land and waters in the Rainy River Watershed from mining claims, mineral leasing, and disposal, locking in protection for land upstream of the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness [S2][S3].

The bill's findings describe sulfide-ore copper mining as a direct, long-term pollution threat: a peer-reviewed study found all 14 operating U.S. copper sulfide mines examined had pipeline spills or accidental releases, and 13 had failures of water collection and treatment systems [S3].

Sulfide mining can produce acid mine drainage — sulfuric acid that leaches copper, lead, and other metals into groundwater and lakes — in a watershed that holds 20 percent of the fresh water in the entire National Forest System [S3].

The bill preserves local mining traditions it deems safe: the Forest Service may still permit removal of sand, gravel, granite, iron ore, and taconite if it would not hurt water quality or forest habitat [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: A sulfide-ore copper mining company that holds leases and exploration interests in the watershed loses its path to mine there. Counties and towns hoping for mining jobs and tax base would not get them; the bill's answer is that tourism jobs would more than make up the difference, but that trade is contested [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Copper mining interests and mining-dependent counties

drawbacks.text: The block applies to copper, nickel, platinum, palladium, gold, and silver — metals used in batteries, electronics, and renewable energy. A permanent withdrawal removes one potential domestic source of those minerals, a real cost at a time of rising demand for domestic critical-minerals supply [S3].
The withdrawal is permanent rather than subject to periodic review, so future generations cannot reconsider the tradeoff even if mining technology or mineral markets change substantially [S3].

Counties in the affected area (Cook, Lake, and Saint Louis) would give up potential mining-related jobs, royalties, and tax revenue, a loss that falls on a specific rural region even if the state's tourism economy gains overall [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — keeping acid mine drainage out of a unique, largely irreversible wilderness and watershed — is backed by the Forest Service's own 2016 finding that the risk was 'unacceptable' and by a 2022 environmental assessment recommending withdrawal [S3]. The main cost is forgone mining development and its jobs in a corner of Minnesota, plus one less domestic source of battery metals. The trade is regional on the cost side and national on the benefit side, and the bill is candid that it chooses the watershed over the mine.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on January 21, 2025 and referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, which has taken no further action on it [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Betty McCollum introduced the bill on January 21, 2025, with 20 initial cosponsors, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Natural Resources [S3][S5].
The bill had 41 cosponsors, all Democrats, as of the most recent cosponsor list [S4].
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — has been recorded since the referral [S5].

The bill would codify an existing administrative decision: in January 2023 the Interior Department issued a public land order withdrawing the same 225,504 acres, and the bill's stated map is the one attached to that order [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one's position has changed: the land remains protected by the 2023 administrative order, which a future administration could reverse, while the bill that would make the protection permanent has not moved [S3][S5].

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo: wilderness protected only by executive order

for.name: Rep. Betty McCollum
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 20 original cosponsors at introduction.

for.name: 41 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, bringing total support to 42 members, all Democrats.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in January 2025 and has not scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it.

sides.party_line_note: All 42 sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats; the Republican-controlled committee of referral has taken no action, and no Republican has cosponsored.

industries.note: The bill removes about 225,504 acres of the Rainy River Watershed from mining claims and mineral leasing, ending the path to mine copper and other metals there. Its interest runs against the public in this bill because the pollution risk it poses — acid mine drainage into a watershed holding 20 percent of the National Forest System's fresh water — is the exact harm the bill exists to prevent [S2][S3].

A permanent withdrawal protects the pristine wilderness the region's canoe-country tourism economy depends on. The bill's findings project 1,500 to 4,600 more jobs and $100 million to $900 million more income over 20 years with a ban than without one [S3].

industries.industry: Traditional iron ore, taconite, and aggregate extraction
industries.note: The bill explicitly allows the Forest Service to keep permitting removal of sand, gravel, granite, iron ore, and taconite in the withdrawn area, as long as it does not harm water quality or forest habitat — sparing Minnesota's established iron range industries from the ban [S3].

analysis.trajectory: With 42 cosponsors, all Democrats, and a referral to a Republican-controlled committee that has not acted, the bill is very unlikely to reach the House floor this Congress. Its practical significance is that the underlying protection now rests on a 2023 administrative order that a future administration can undo; without a statute, that protection remains reversible, and there is no sign this Congress will change that.
